 What is Continuous Recording and Where to Save it
 Continuous recording means that the cameras can record 24/7 without interruption, regardless of whether motion is detected. Reolink currently supports continuous recording in the following ways: 
 1. microSD card 
 2. Reolink NVR/Home Hub 
 3. Local Recording to PC through Reolink Client 
 4. FTP Continuous Recording 
 5. 3rd Party Software 
 1. microSD card 
 You can install a microSD card in the camera to store continuous recordings. The table below lists the models that support continuous recording to a microSD card.

 2. Reolink NVR/Home Hub 
 In addition to centralized camera management, Reolink NVR and Home Hub are local storage devices, supporting large local storage options. To enable continuous recording on the Reolink NVR/Home Hub, you need to confirm a few compatibility requirements first. 
 The camera support continuous recording.

Reolink identifies only certain battery-powered exceptions, including the Altas and TrackMix LTE Plus lines. Eufy’s eufyCam 3 and 3C documentation also says they do not support constant recording.
 FAQ 
 What is the best home security camera without a subscription?
 The best choice depends on the installation. The Reolink Argus 4 Pro is best for wide-angle battery coverage, the Tapo C120 is the best inexpensive plug-in option, the eufyCam S3 Pro is best for a solar multi-camera system, and the Reolink Duo 3 PoE is best for wired 24/7 recording.
 Can security cameras record without Wi-Fi or internet?
 Some cameras can continue recording to local storage after losing internet access, but initial setup and features such as remote viewing, notifications, account authentication, and updates may require internet. Fully offline operation is not guaranteed.
 Do battery security cameras record 24/7?
 Usually not. Most battery cameras sleep between events and record only when motion or another trigger occurs. A plug-in or PoE camera is the safer choice for continuous recording.
 Is local camera storage safer than cloud storage?
 Local storage gives you control and avoids recurring fees, but it is vulnerable if the camera, memory card, or hub is stolen or damaged. Cloud storage provides an off-site copy, usually at an additional cost. Exporting important clips to a separate computer or NAS provides another option.
 The Bottom Line 
 For most buyers, choose the TP-Link Tapo C120 if you have a power outlet and want inexpensive continuous recording, or the Reolink Argus 4 Pro if you need broad battery-powered coverage.  What is a PoE NVR camera system and how does it differ from Wi-Fi cameras?
 A PoE NVR system runs a single Ethernet cable to each camera that carries both power and data back to a network video recorder (NVR), which films every camera continuously to a built-in hard drive. Unlike battery or Wi-Fi cameras that record motion clips to the cloud, a PoE NVR kit records 24/7 to storage you own, with no monthly fee. The trade-off is the cabling — you run Ethernet to each camera location during install.

 PoE vs wireless security cameras — which should I buy?
 Choose a wired PoE NVR system if you own your home, can run Ethernet, and want continuous 24/7 recording with no monthly fee. Choose wireless battery cameras if you rent, can't run cable, or want a faster install — they record locally too, but in motion clips rather than continuously. The wired kits in this guide trade install effort for round-the-clock recording you fully own.
 Do I need a separate PoE switch for an NVR system?
 Not for the cameras included in these kits — each NVR has built-in PoE ports that power and connect the bundled cameras directly. You only need a separate PoE switch if you add cameras beyond the NVR's port count or want to power cameras from your main network rather than the recorder. Doorbell Cameras Without a Subscription

Four doorbells save video locally with no subscription: the Reolink Video Doorbell WiFi, eufy Video Doorbell C30, Tapo D210 and Blink Video Doorbell.

The Reolink Video Doorbell WiFi hardwired kit pairs with the Reolink Home Hub Mini to store footage locally on a microSD card up to 1TB. Reolink includes motion detection, person detection, and package detection on this model without charging recurring monthly storage fees.

The eufy Video Doorbell C30 runs on a 5,000 mAh rechargeable battery and accepts a microSD card up to 128GB with no monthly fee. The C30 offers human and motion detection and can link with a eufy HomeBase S280 or HomeBase S380 hub.

TP-Link sells the Tapo D210 battery doorbell, which writes recorded video events directly to an on-device microSD card. Tapo says AI person detection alerts are free. Tapo also says Tapo Care cloud storage is optional and never required.

Amazon's Blink Video Doorbell supports local storage when paired with an optional Blink Sync Module 2. The Sync Module 2 saves motion clips to a connected USB flash drive without requiring a Blink subscription plan.

According to Ring's camera features documentation, a Ring doorbell without a plan gets Live View and motion alerts but saves no video history. For Ring's plan prices, read our analysis of Ring subscription costs. To compare other doorbell brands, see our guide to Ring alternatives.

What You Give Up Without a Plan

Operating a security camera without a subscription saves money, but requires you to manage physical hardware risks and storage limits yourself.

No automated off-site video backup: If an intruder steals your camera or breaks into your home and takes your recorder, your footage is gone. A cloud plan such as eufy Security Cloud Backup keeps 30 days of video off-site, so a copy survives if the camera is smashed.
Hardware management and drive maintenance: Memory cards and spinning hard drives eventually wear out or run out of capacity. You must format storage media, replace degraded drives, and verify that your system is actively writing files to local disks.
Paid detection on Wyze and Arlo: Wyze and Arlo record to microSD cards for free on supported cameras. Person, package and vehicle alerts need a paid plan. Wyze charges $2.99 per month for Cam Plus with person detection. Arlo Secure Plus starts at $7.99 per month for smart motion identification.

You can learn more about protecting personal electronics across your household in our guide on how to protect your privacy online.

Local Storage Options Explained

Local storage security camera systems rely on three primary hardware configurations: standalone microSD cards, centralized network video recorders (NVRs), or proprietary base station hubs.

MicroSD cards fit directly inside an individual camera housing. As noted by Reolink's subscription guide, most Reolink cameras carry a slot accepting cards up to 256GB or 512GB. TP-Link Tapo cameras also support cards up to 512GB for 24-hour continuous recording. A microSD card is lost if someone takes the camera off the wall.

Network video recorders (NVRs) and digital video recorders (DVRs) store footage on central hard drives inside your home. According to Lorex's recorder documentation, an NVR works with Internet Protocol (IP) security cameras connected using Ethernet cables and Power-over-Ethernet (PoE). A DVR works with analog cameras connected over coaxial cabling. NVR systems support continuous 24/7 video capture across multiple camera channels while keeping the physical drives secured inside your home.

Base stations and proprietary home hubs bridge wireless cameras to centralized local drives. The eufy HomeBase S380 costs $199.99 and accepts any 5V 2.5-inch hard drive or solid-state drive with a SATA interface, expanding up to 16TB. The HomeBase processes person, vehicle, and pet recognition locally while keeping storage drives indoors. Similarly, Amazon's Blink Sync Module 2 connects Blink wireless cameras to a local USB drive between 1GB and 256GB with zero subscription fees.

For high-capacity deployments, Ubiquiti UniFi Protect operates cameras on a UniFi Console with zero software licensing costs. UniFi Protect uses edge computing for on-camera artificial intelligence, keeping all Smart Detections and surveillance footage on local hardware. For a camera network that homeowners do not control, see our explainer on Flock cameras.

How to Pick by Home Type

Match the storage type to your home and its wiring.

Apartments and rental units: Battery-powered hardware with local memory cards minimizes wall damage and avoids complex network setups. The eufy Video Doorbell C30 or a TP-Link Tapo camera with an onboard microSD card provides person detection with no monthly fee.
Single-family homes with existing Wi-Fi: Centralized base station systems provide larger storage capacity without running Ethernet cables through attic spaces. A eufy HomeBase S380 paired with wireless outdoor cameras keeps recorded video clips safe inside your home on an expandable SATA drive. For a head-to-head brand breakdown, see our guide comparing eufy vs Reolink.
New construction or detached properties: Hardwired Power-over-Ethernet (PoE) cameras paired with an indoor NVR deliver continuous 24/7 recording. Reolink NVRs and Lorex NVRs record to a local hard drive with no monthly fee.
Enthusiast networks and homelabs: Ubiquiti UniFi Protect provides professional surveillance software with zero licensing fees. UniFi consoles process smart object detections locally and manage extensive camera arrays across private local networks. For broader hardware ideas, read our overview of building a dumb home.
Who Should Stay on a Cloud Subscription

Staying on a paid cloud subscription makes sense if you do not want to manage local storage drives, format memory cards, or worry about equipment theft. Ring's paid plans keep up to 180 days of cloud video history, so a copy survives if the camera is stolen.

For a related privacy question about smart speakers, read our report on is Alexa always listening. Ring Edge local processing on the Ring Alarm Pro requires an eligible Ring subscription just to save clips to a local microSD card. If you already pay for full-home security monitoring contracts that bundle cloud video storage, moving to standalone local cameras may introduce unnecessary administrative work.

What Would Change Our Verdict

If Reolink, eufy, or TP-Link Tapo introduces mandatory monthly subscription fees to access on-device person and vehicle detection, we will remove them from our recommended list. If Wyze or Arlo eliminates subscription paywalls for person detection on cameras equipped with microSD cards, we will elevate their standing for budget shoppers. If Ring or Google Nest introduces standalone local storage options that operate without an active subscription plan, their hardware will become viable alternatives for privacy-focused homeowners.

 Frequently Asked Questions
 What is the best security camera with local storage in 2026? The eufyCam S3 Pro with HomeBase 3 is our overall pick — a 4K solar-powered system that stores footage on the hub's 16GB of built-in storage, expandable up to 16TB with a standard hard drive, with no monthly fee. The Reolink Argus 4 Pro is the best single wire-free camera with a microSD slot (up to 512GB), a Reolink PoE NVR kit is the best 24/7 whole-home option, and the Wyze Cam v4 brings free continuous local recording down to about $36.
 What are the three types of local storage for security cameras? MicroSD cards inside the camera itself (Wyze, Reolink, Tapo) are the simplest and cheapest; a hub or base station (eufy HomeBase 3, Blink Sync Module 2) stores clips from several cameras in one indoor box that a thief can't grab off the wall; and an NVR or DVR (Reolink, Lorex, Amcrest kits) records every camera 24/7 to a multi-terabyte hard drive. MicroSD suits one or two cameras, a hub suits a wire-free multi-camera home, and an NVR is the gold standard for continuous whole-property coverage.
 Are local storage security cameras as good as cloud cameras? For recording quality, yes — the video is identical; only where it's saved differs. Local storage wins on cost (no $50–$200-a-year plan), privacy (footage never leaves your home), and resilience (an internet outage doesn't stop an NVR or microSD card recording). Cloud wins on off-site backup: if a burglar steals the camera and the card inside it, cloud copies survive. Hub and NVR systems split the difference by keeping the storage hidden indoors, and most local-first brands offer optional cloud as a backup layer.
 Do local storage cameras still send alerts to my phone? Yes. Every pick in this guide sends motion notifications and live views through its app over your home internet exactly like a cloud camera — the difference is only where the recorded clip is stored. Note the distinction between storage and connectivity: these cameras still use Wi-Fi or Ethernet to talk to your phone. If you need a camera that works with no internet at all, see our no-WiFi camera guide.
 What happens if a thief steals the camera or its SD card? That's the one real weakness of in-camera microSD storage — the evidence can walk away with the camera. Three defenses: mount cameras high and out of easy reach; prefer a hub or NVR system (eufy HomeBase 3, Blink Sync Module 2, or any NVR kit) where footage lives on a device hidden inside the house; or enable the optional cloud backup that brands like Reolink, eufy and Wyze offer as a second layer. An NVR in a locked closet is effectively as theft-proof as the cloud.
 Which security camera brands don't charge a monthly fee for local storage? eufy, Reolink, Lorex, ANNKE, Amcrest, TP-Link Tapo and Wyze all record locally for free — you pay once for the camera (and the card or drive) and never again. Blink stores clips free on a Sync Module 2 USB drive, though some AI features need its paid plan. The brands that push hardest toward a subscription are Ring, Nest and Arlo, which keep recorded history in the cloud — see our no-subscription camera guide for the full fee-free rundown.

 What does local storage mean for a security camera? 
 Local storage means the camera footage is recorded somewhere you control rather than being stored exclusively in a vendor’s cloud. The storage location can be a microSD card inside the camera, a dedicated hub, a local NVR, a UniFi console, or a NAS.

 How should you install and configure a local-storage camera? 
 Define the evidence target. Decide whether you need a general overview, a recognizable face, a license plate, package activity, or continuous coverage. Resolution alone does not determine evidence quality; lens angle, zoom, lighting, mounting position, compression, and subject distance matter.
 Select the architecture. Use microSD for a small motion-recording installation, a hub for compatible battery cameras, an NVR for several wired cameras or 24/7 recording, and a NAS or self-hosted platform only when you are prepared to manage compatibility and networking.
 Verify exact compatibility. Check the camera model, hardware revision, firmware, hub or NVR model, maximum card or drive capacity, supported camera count, and supported third-party protocols. Do not generalize compatibility across an entire brand.
 Plan power and networking. PoE cameras need Ethernet routing plus a PoE switch, injector, or compatible NVR. Battery cameras need a mounting location that supports reliable wireless communication and practical charging or solar conditions.
 Configure recording mode. Choose motion, scheduled, or 24/7 recording deliberately. Confirm whether the selected camera supports the mode you want, and set overwrite behavior so the system does not stop unexpectedly when storage fills.
 Configure remote access and privacy. Review account requirements, remote-viewing paths, thumbnail notifications, cloud backup, and local-AI settings. Disable optional cloud features if they conflict with your privacy requirements.
 Test retrieval. Trigger a recording, disconnect the internet if offline operation matters, retrieve a clip locally, verify timestamps, and confirm that notifications and exports behave as expected.
 Plan maintenance. Inspect recording status, replace high-write storage when necessary, test the UPS, keep firmware current, and export important clips to a separate location.

 Frequently Asked Questions 
 Can security cameras with local storage work without a subscription?
 Yes, local recording can usually work without paying for a cloud-storage subscription, but “no subscription” does not always mean “fully offline.” Remote viewing, accounts, thumbnail notifications, cloud backup, and other optional services may still use the internet. Confirm the exact model’s settings and requirements.
 Are battery security cameras suitable for 24/7 local recording?
 Wired PoE cameras and local NVRs are generally better suited to demanding 24/7 recording because they have continuous power and centralized storage. Battery cameras such as eufyCam models are better suited to wire-free installation and event-based recording unless the manufacturer explicitly supports the required continuous-recording behavior.
 What happens to local footage if someone steals the camera?
 A camera-local microSD card may be stolen with the camera, while a hub or NVR placed elsewhere can preserve footage after camera theft. A hub or NVR can also be stolen or suffer drive failure, so important clips should be exported to a separate location.
 Is local camera storage the same as a backup?
 No. Local storage is one copy of the footage, not automatically a backup. RAID can improve storage availability on supported recorders, but a separate copy is still needed to protect against theft, corruption, accidental deletion, fire, or failure affecting the entire recorder.

 Understanding local storage options
 Not all local storage is created equal. Here is what each type means in practice and when you should choose it.
 MicroSD cards
 The simplest option. The camera has a card slot, you insert a microSD card, and it records directly to it. No network configuration needed. The downsides are limited capacity (typically 128GB to 512GB), the risk of losing footage if the camera is stolen, and the need to physically remove the card if you want to access footage without the app. Best for single-camera setups where simplicity is the priority.
 NVR (Network Video Recorder)
 An NVR is a dedicated box designed specifically for security cameras. It typically has PoE ports to power cameras directly, a large hard drive for weeks or months of recording, and a simple interface for playback and export. Reolink's NVR system pairs perfectly with the RLC-810A. Best for buyers who want a professional-grade multi-camera setup without getting into DIY NAS territory.
 NAS (Network Attached Storage)
 A NAS is a general-purpose network drive — think of it as a private server in your closet. Cameras that support RTSP or ONVIF can stream footage to a NAS running surveillance software like Synology Surveillance Station, Blue Iris, or Frigate. This is the most flexible option and the best choice for Home Assistant users, but it requires more technical setup. The RLC-810A and Amcrest AD410 are the best NAS-compatible cameras in this guide.
 How much storage do you actually need?
 This depends on two things: resolution and recording mode. Here are rough estimates for a single camera.
 Event-only recording at 2K: 64GB card lasts approximately 5 to 7 days
 Event-only recording at 4K: 128GB card lasts approximately 4 to 6 days
 Continuous recording at 2K: 128GB card lasts approximately 4 to 5 days
 Continuous recording at 4K: 128GB card lasts approximately 1 to 2 days
 NVR with 2TB drive at 4K: approximately 10 to 14 days per camera
 If you need more than a week of retention at high resolution, microSD alone will not cut it. That is where NVR or NAS setups become essential.
 Continuous vs event-based recording
 Continuous recording captures everything, all the time. You never miss a moment, but you burn through storage quickly and spend more time scrubbing through footage to find what matters. Best for high-security areas or when paired with large NVR/NAS storage.
 Event-based recording only saves clips when motion or AI detection triggers. It uses far less storage and makes reviewing footage faster, but there is always a slight risk of missing the first second of an event while the camera wakes up and starts recording. Every camera in this guide supports event-based recording, and it is the right choice for most homes.
 RTSP and ONVIF: why they matter
 RTSP (Real Time Streaming Protocol) and ONVIF (Open Network Video Interface Forum) are open standards that let your camera talk to third-party software. If a camera supports RTSP, you can pull its video feed into nearly any recording platform — Blue Iris on Windows, Frigate on a Raspberry Pi or Docker, Synology Surveillance Station on a NAS, or Home Assistant for full smart home integration.
 This matters because it means you are not locked into the manufacturer's app or cloud service. If Reolink or Amcrest shut down tomorrow, your cameras would still record to your own hardware. The TP-Link Tapo C120, Reolink RLC-810A, and Amcrest AD410 all support these protocols. The Reolink Argus 4 Pro and eufy SoloCam S340 do not, which is their biggest limitation for power users.
 Common mistakes to avoid
 Buying a cheap SD card: Not all microSD cards are equal. Security cameras write data constantly, which destroys low-quality cards quickly. Buy a card rated for "high endurance" or "surveillance" use — Samsung PRO Endurance and SanDisk High Endurance are the two most reliable options.
 Assuming "local storage supported" means "no subscription needed": Some cameras (Ring, for example) have SD card slots but still require a subscription to access useful AI features. Every camera in this guide runs its AI detection free.
 Ignoring overwrite settings: Most cameras overwrite the oldest footage when storage is full. Make sure you know how much retention time your card gives you and check that loop recording is enabled — otherwise the camera just stops recording when the card is full.
 Skipping the PoE option for multi-camera setups: Wi-Fi cameras are easy to install one at a time, but four or five Wi-Fi cameras on one network can create congestion. If you are planning three or more outdoor cameras, seriously consider PoE with the RLC-810A and an NVR.
 Not testing your microSD card after installation: Insert the card, let the camera record for a day, then check that playback works. A surprising number of buyers discover weeks later that their card was not formatted correctly or was counterfeit.
 How to choose the right one
 If you want the simplest, best all-around wireless camera with local storage and no fees, buy the Reolink Argus 4 Pro . If you want a solar-powered camera that covers a wide area with pan and tilt, the eufy SoloCam S340 is excellent. If you are on a tight budget and want maximum storage capacity, the TP-Link Tapo C120 is extraordinary value. If you are building a multi-camera system with centralized NVR or NAS recording, the Reolink RLC-810A is the obvious foundation. And if you specifically need a front door camera with real local storage and no subscription, the Amcrest AD410 is one of the very few doorbells that delivers it.

 It depends on resolution and recording mode. For event-only recording at 2K, a 64GB card typically holds 5 to 7 days of clips. For continuous recording at 4K, a 128GB card may only last 1 to 2 days. If you want longer retention with continuous recording, look at cameras that support NAS or NVR storage like the Reolink RLC-810A, which can record to a dedicated hard drive system with terabytes of space. 
 Is local storage more secure than cloud storage for security cameras?
 In most practical ways, yes. Local storage means your footage never leaves your network, so it cannot be exposed in a cloud data breach or accessed by the camera company. The tradeoff is that if someone steals the camera and the SD card inside it, you lose the footage. The best approach is a camera that supports both local and remote backup — for example, recording to microSD while also syncing to a NAS on your home network. 
 What is the difference between microSD, NVR, and NAS storage for security cameras?
 MicroSD is the simplest option: a small memory card inserted directly into the camera. NVR (Network Video Recorder) is a dedicated box designed specifically for security cameras — it manages recording, playback, and storage across multiple cameras. NAS (Network Attached Storage) is a general-purpose network drive that some cameras can write to via RTSP or ONVIF protocols. NVR is easiest for multi-camera setups, NAS is most flexible, and microSD is best for single-camera installs. 
 Do security cameras with local storage still need Wi-Fi?
 Most do, yes. Wi-Fi is needed for live viewing on your phone, receiving motion alerts, and adjusting settings remotely. However, the actual footage recording happens locally on the SD card or NVR regardless of whether your internet connection is working. This is a major advantage over cloud-only cameras, which stop recording entirely if your internet goes down. 
 Can I use a security camera with local storage without any app or account?
 Some cameras support this via RTSP and ONVIF protocols. The TP-Link Tapo C120 also supports ONVIF. Fully wireless cameras like the Reolink Argus 4 Pro generally require the app for initial setup but can then record to SD card independently. 
 What happens to local storage footage when the camera loses power?
 Footage already saved to a microSD card or NVR is preserved — it does not disappear when power is lost. The camera simply stops recording new footage until power returns. Battery-powered cameras like the Reolink Argus 4 Pro and eufy SoloCam S340 have an advantage here because they continue recording during power outages. For wired cameras, a small UPS (uninterruptible power supply) can keep them running through short outages. 
 The bottom line
 You should not have to pay a monthly fee to watch footage from a camera you already own. Every camera in this guide records locally, runs AI detection for free, and works without a cloud subscription. The Reolink Argus 4 Pro is the best overall pick for most people — 4K quality, solar charging, and completely wireless installation with zero ongoing costs. For budget buyers, the TP-Link Tapo C120 at $35 is one of the best deals in smart home security right now.  The Tapo C220 is an indoor pan/tilt camera: 2K QHD (2560x1440), 360 degree pan coverage, 850nm infrared night vision to about 40 ft, and a long AI detection list that runs locally (person, pet, vehicle, baby cry, glass-break, bark and meow detection). It records to a microSD card up to 512GB. Power is a 9V DC wall adapter, so it is wired, indoor, and always on, with support for continuous recording to the card.
 The paywall line at Tapo is drawn at cloud: Tapo Care (subscription, first month free per TP-Link) adds cloud storage and one notification upgrade that TP-Link explicitly labels as a Tapo Care feature: notifications with a snapshot preview. Plain notifications, all AI detections, RTSP/ONVIF streaming to your own recorder, and full microSD recording are free.
 TP-Link does not list a price on tp-link.com; the buy button routes to Amazon, so the price you pay is a retailer street price.
 Lorex: NVR systems with no fees at all
 Lorex is the most complete no-subscription approach in this roundup: a wired NVR system where footage lives on a hard drive in your house. The representative system here (N91062 Fusion series) includes an 8-channel 4K NVR with a 2TB security-grade hard drive, expandable to a maximum of 16TB, plus four wired 4K (8MP) PoE cameras with a 127 degree diagonal field of view, color night vision, IP67 housings, and built-in mics and speakers.
 Lorex's stated position on the product page is no monthly fees, with all premium features included: person, vehicle, face, animal, and package detection all run locally at no extra cost. Remote app viewing is free (Lorex recommends at least 6Mbps upload for reasonable remote video). Lorex does sell optional cloud plans, but for select Wi-Fi cameras, not as a requirement for these wired NVR systems.
 Lorex does not publish a price for this system: as of August 2026 the product page states it is only available for purchase by contacting the Lorex sales team. The honest trade still applies: a wired NVR system costs substantially more up front than a single Wi-Fi camera and requires running Ethernet cable, in exchange for zero recurring cost and continuous recording. These systems also keep recording with no internet at all, which we cover in security cameras that work without WiFi .
 Amcrest: the tinkerer's pick
 Amcrest sells traditional IP cameras. The IP8M-2496EB-V2 is a 4K (8MP, 3840x2160) outdoor bullet camera with PoE or 12V DC power, IP67 weatherproofing, 98 ft infrared night vision, and H.265 compression.
 What makes Amcrest different is how many free storage paths it supports, all listed on the product page: microSD card in the camera, Amcrest NVRs, Synology and QNAP NAS boxes, FTP, and third-party PC software including Blue Iris. If you want your camera footage on a NAS you already own, this is the shortest path in this roundup. Amcrest Cloud exists as an optional remote storage service.
 One gap: the product page confirms microSD recording but does not publish a maximum supported card capacity for this model, so we list that as not published. Listed at $99.99 as of August 2026, the cheapest 4K option covered here.
 How to choose between SD card, hub, and NVR
 MicroSD in the camera (Reolink Argus, Tapo, Amcrest) is the cheapest and simplest, with one real weakness: if someone steals the camera, they steal your footage with it. Cards also wear out with continuous rewriting.
 A hub (Eufy HomeBase, Reolink Home Hub) moves storage inside your house, aggregates multiple cameras, and on Eufy unlocks better AI. It costs more up front and locks you into one brand's ecosystem.
 An NVR (Lorex, Amcrest) is the most robust: terabytes of storage, continuous 24/7 recording, wired reliability, and no cloud dependence. It is also the most expensive and the most work to install.
 Whichever you pick, be clear-eyed about what a camera does not do: it documents events and notifies your phone. If an intruder alarm that summons help matters to your situation, cameras alone do not provide it, and turning off notifications to reduce false alerts quietly turns off the only response layer you have. The cost math of adding monitoring on top is in home security cost per month .
 Cameras also do not detect a door or window opening; that is an alarm system's job. If you want one around a no-fee camera setup, Cove vs SimpliSafe compares two no-contract systems that price monitoring by the day, and ADT monitoring cost sets out what ADT publishes for its plans and what it does not.
 How long footage is kept depends on the plan and the storage; how long security cameras keep footage lists the cloud history for each brand.
 Frequently asked questions
 Do any of these cameras secretly require a subscription later? No, not for recording and playback on the models covered here. All five makers state local recording works with no monthly fee. What paid plans add is cloud backup and, in Tapo's case, snapshot previews in notifications. Features can change with firmware and policy updates, so check the maker's current spec page before buying. 
 Which no-subscription camera records 24/7? Of the models covered here, the wired options: Tapo C220 (to microSD), the Lorex NVR system, and the Amcrest IP8M-2496EB-V2 (to NVR or NAS). Battery cameras like the Reolink Argus 4 Pro and Eufy SoloCam S340 only record motion-triggered clips; Eufy's own FAQ confirms battery cameras cannot do 24/7 recording even with a HomeBase. 
 Is footage on a microSD card safe? It is private (it never leaves the camera), but it is not theft-proof: stealing the camera takes the footage with it. If that risk matters at your location, prefer a hub or NVR that stores footage inside your house, or use a maker's optional cloud plan as a backup layer. 
 Can these cameras call the police? No. Self-hosted cameras send phone notifications only; no monitoring center sees your alerts, and nobody dispatches on your behalf. If you want dispatch, you need a monitored alarm service, which is a separate decision from camera storage.

 The best home security camera for most houses is the eufy SoloCam S340 . It charges from its own solar panel, pans and tilts across a full circle, and writes every recording to storage inside the camera body, so nothing stands between you and your own footage. If you can run a cable instead, the Reolink RLC-811A does more for less.
 Almost every camera roundup ranks on resolution and night vision, then mentions storage in a footnote. That is backwards. The specification that decides what a camera costs you over five years, what it does when the internet drops, and whether you can watch yesterday afternoon at all is a boring one: where the video is written when the camera sees something . Answer that first and most of this category sorts itself out.
 The organizing question. There are exactly three answers to “where does the footage live?” — on the camera, on a box in your house, or in a company's data center. The first two are hardware decisions you pay for once. The third is a subscription decision you pay for every month, for as long as you own the camera. Two of the eight cameras below record nothing you can watch later unless you are paying, and both of them are excellent hardware. That is the trade this page exists to make legible.
 The best home security cameras, compared
 Six columns, none of them marketing. Read the second and third across before you read anything else: they are the two that change what the camera costs after the box is open.
 Compiled from manufacturer specifications and published support documentation, July 2026. No prices appear in this table; prices are live on each pick above. Model Storage location Works with no plan? Continuous or event-only Power Resolution Offline behavior

 Where the footage lives decides everything else
 Three storage models exist in this category. Each one sets your monthly cost, your behavior during an outage, and what happens to the recording if the camera itself disappears. Pick the model first and the shortlist writes itself. We have a longer treatment of the trade in local storage vs cloud security cameras , but the short version is below.
 1. On the camera
 A microSD card or fixed internal storage inside the camera body. The eufy SoloCam S340, both Reolinks, both Tapos and the eufy Indoor Cam S350 all work this way. Cost after purchase: a card, once. The footage never leaves your property unless you export it. The limitation is the honest one nobody in this category prints: a camera that is removed from the wall takes its recordings with it. If the camera is the only copy and the camera is gone, so is the evidence.
 2. On a base station or recorder in your house
 A hub with a real drive in it — a eufy HomeBase, a Reolink NVR — sitting somewhere less obvious than the camera. This is the same local-ownership economics with the removal problem solved, because the recorder is indoors and the camera is only a sensor. It costs more up front and it means finding somewhere with mains power and airflow for a box. Retention stops being a plan tier and becomes a drive size.
 3. In the manufacturer's cloud
 The Arlo Pro 5S and the Ring Outdoor Cam. Both are genuinely good hardware — Ring has the most reliable notifications in the category and Arlo has the best sensor of the eight — and on neither one will you be able to watch a clip from this morning unless you are paying. This is not a hidden term; both companies state it. It is simply stated quietly, after you have bought the camera. Over five years the plan usually exceeds what the hardware cost, which is the arithmetic we lay out in the subscription cost comparison .
 Read this before buying any cloud-only camera. “Works without a subscription” is used by several brands to mean “you can still see the live view and get a notification.” It does not mean the camera saves anything. If the reason you are buying a camera is to look at what happened while you were out, a live-only camera does not do that job at any price.
 Continuous recording versus event clips
 Continuous recording writes a rolling 24-hour timeline you can scrub through. Event recording writes a clip when something triggers detection, and nothing in between. The gap between them is larger than it sounds, because event detection has a wake-up delay: a battery camera is asleep until its passive infrared sensor fires, and the first second or two of the approach is often already over by the time the sensor is streaming.
 This is not a price feature. It is a power feature. Keeping an image sensor and an encoder running continuously is a constant draw of several watts, which no battery or solar panel of this size sustains. Reolink states the constraint plainly on its own battery line, and it is true of every battery camera made by anyone: they record events, and that is what they are for. Among the picks here, the two that record continuously are both mains-fed — the Tapo 2K+ Wired on a socket and the Reolink RLC-811A on Power over Ethernet.
 So the real decision order runs: can I get power to this spot? If yes, buy a wired camera and get a continuous timeline. If no, accept event clips and buy the solar camera that will actually stay charged where you are putting it.
 Power is the constraint that decides the shortlist
 Four power models appear above, and they are not interchangeable.
 Power over Ethernet. One Cat6 cable carries power and data. Nothing to charge, ever, and the network path does not depend on Wi-Fi reaching the far corner of the garden. The cost is that you have to pull the cable and own a PoE switch or injector.
 Mains socket. Cheapest route to continuous recording. Requires an outdoor-rated supply within reach of the mount, which is frequently a bigger job than the camera costs.
 Solar and battery. Install once and forget, but only where the panel gets genuine direct sun. This is the single most common outdoor-camera regret and it gets a full section in our outdoor camera roundup .
 Battery alone. Fine indoors or on a low-traffic approach. On a busy front elevation, a battery camera triggered forty times a day is a ladder trip every few weeks.
 Resolution is the specification people over-buy
 4K sounds like the answer and often is not. Detail at distance is set by how many pixels land on the subject, which is a function of sensor resolution and field of view and distance. A 4K camera with a very wide lens covering a whole driveway can put fewer pixels on a face at twelve meters than a 2K camera with a narrower lens aimed at the gate. This is why the RLC-811A ranks second overall on a page where a 3K camera is first: its 5x zoom is optical, so the pixels are gathered at the subject rather than interpolated afterward.
 Higher resolution also costs storage and bandwidth in direct proportion. A 4K continuous stream fills a card several times faster than 2K, which means shorter retention on the same card, and on a battery camera it means fewer events between charges. If a camera is watching a side passage three meters wide, 2K is the correct specification and the money is better spent on getting power to the mounting point.
 What a camera cannot do
 A camera records an event. It does not prevent one. That distinction is worth being blunt about, because the category sells hard in the other direction, and a household that has installed four cameras often believes it has done more than it has.
 Three concrete limits:
 It only knows what is in frame. A camera covering the front approach has nothing to say about the back door, the garage side door or a ground-floor window on the flank of the house.
 Detection is a filter, not an understanding. Motion and person detection fire on movement of a certain shape. They do not know whether the person is the neighbor collecting a parcel or someone who should not be there, and no setting makes them know.
 Notification is not response. A clip arriving on your phone during a meeting is a record, not an action.
 What a camera at the front of the house cannot tell you is that a door has just opened. A contact sensor can, for a fraction of the price, and it does it as a binary fact rather than as a judgment about pixels: the magnet and the reed switch separated, so the door is open. That is a different and complementary kind of information, it arrives instantly, it does not depend on lighting, and on a Thread or Zigbee sensor it runs locally with no cloud in the path. If you are covering a house rather than a driveway, read our door and window sensor roundup alongside this page — the two purchases cover different failure modes and the sensor side costs a fraction of the camera side.
 Which of these you should actually choose between
 Eight cameras is a long list to hold in your head. For most people the real decision is between three of them:
 You cannot run a cable. eufy SoloCam S340, if and only if the mounting spot sees direct sun for a few hours a day. Otherwise the Reolink Argus PT Ultra with the same caveat, or a battery camera you accept charging.
 You can run a cable. Reolink RLC-811A. Continuous recording, optical zoom, no charging, no plan, and it drops straight into Home Assistant, Frigate or Blue Iris over RTSP and ONVIF.
 You want the least expensive thing that still records all day. The Tapo 2K+ Wired, on any socket. It is the cheapest camera here that gives you a continuous timeline instead of clips.
 If you have already decided that a subscription is not happening, our cameras without a subscription shortlist filters this same field to the models where every core function is free forever. And if your shortlist has come down to two brands rather than two cameras, Ring vs eufy is the head-to-head that settles it, because the two companies sit on opposite sides of the storage question.
 How we picked
 Products we claim to have tested: 0. Everyone in this category tells you they lived with a dozen cameras for a month. We have not, and we say so. What we do instead is compile the published specification, read the manufacturer's own support documentation for the parts they would rather you found out later, compute what the hardware costs to keep running, and cite all of it. Rankings weight storage location, usability with no plan, image system, power model and ecosystem openness.  How to choose a home security camera
 Work through these in order. Doing them out of order is how people end up with a solar camera on a shaded wall or a wired camera two meters from the nearest socket.
 Step 1 — choose the mounting position before the camera
 Stand where the camera will go and look at what it sees. A camera high on a gable gets a beautiful view of the tops of people's heads and no usable faces. A camera at head height gets faces and is within reach of anyone standing on the path. The compromise most installers settle on is roughly 2.5 to 3 meters, angled down about fifteen degrees, which keeps faces in frame and puts the body just past casual reach. Note what is available at that spot: a socket, a route for a cable, or several hours of direct sun. That note is your shortlist.
 Step 2 — decide where the recording goes
 Card in the camera is the cheapest and simplest, and it fails if the camera is taken. Base station or NVR indoors costs more up front and solves that. Cloud solves it too and charges you monthly forever. There is no option that is cheap, robust against theft of the camera, and free — pick which of the three you are willing to give up.
 Step 3 — match the camera to the power you actually have
 If a socket or an Ethernet run is available, buy a wired camera and take the continuous timeline. If neither is, buy solar and check the sun exposure honestly, in winter, at the actual mounting point. If the spot has no sun either, buy a battery camera and accept a charging cycle; do not buy a solar camera and hope.
 What actually decides the price
 Four things, roughly in order of how much they move the number: the lens and sensor system (optical zoom and a second telephoto lens are expensive; more megapixels on the same wide lens is cheap), the power system (an integrated solar panel and a large cell cost real money), the enclosure and mount, and the on-device processing. What does not move the hardware price is storage, because on a local-recording camera storage is a card you buy separately, and on a cloud camera the storage cost has been moved out of the purchase price and into a monthly line item. That relocation is the entire commercial design of this category.
 The mistake buyers make
 Buying the camera first and discovering the power situation second. The order above exists because the mounting position eliminates most of the field before you have looked at a single specification. The second most common mistake is buying one camera for a whole house: a single camera covers one approach, and a house has three or four. The budget question is usually not “which camera” but “how many cameras of which grade,” and four competent 2K cameras beat one 4K camera pointed at the front door.
 Buy the right card, and buy it once
 A camera writing continuously is one of the harshest workloads consumer flash sees: sustained sequential writes, all day, for years, in an enclosure that reaches high temperatures in summer. Standard cards are specified for cameras and phones that write in bursts. Look for a card sold specifically for continuous video or surveillance use and check the capacity the manufacturer supports before ordering, because cameras have a maximum card size and exceeding it produces a card the camera silently will not use.
 The five-year arithmetic
 The comparison people run in the shop is hardware price against hardware price. The comparison that matters is hardware plus five years of whatever the camera needs to keep doing its job. A local-storage camera's five-year cost is the camera plus a card. A cloud camera's five-year cost is the camera plus sixty monthly payments, and on a multi-camera plan that figure compounds with every camera you add. We keep the brand-by-brand version of that table on the subscription costs compared page rather than quoting a figure here, because plan pricing changes and a number in prose goes stale where a maintained table does not.

 Questions
 Frequently asked
 Do home security cameras work without wifi? + Partly. A camera with local storage keeps recording to its card or its base station with the internet down, so the footage is there when you get home. What you lose is everything remote: push notifications, live view from your phone and cloud backup. A cloud-only camera loses all of that plus the recording itself, because with no connection there is nowhere for the clip to go. A wired camera on your own network is the strongest case — the Reolink RLC-811A keeps streaming over the LAN to a recorder or to Home Assistant even when the connection to the outside world is gone.
 Which security cameras have no monthly fee? + Any camera that writes to storage you own. Among the picks here that is the eufy SoloCam S340, both Reolink models, both Tapo models and the eufy Indoor Cam S350 — every core function including recording, playback and notifications works with no plan. The Arlo Pro 5S and the Ring Outdoor Cam both require a plan before any recorded video is retained. See the local-storage camera shortlist for the filtered list.
 Is a 4K security camera worth it over 2K? + It depends entirely on distance and lens. 4K helps when the subject is far away and the lens is not so wide that the extra pixels are spread across a whole street. On a side passage or a porch, 2K resolves faces perfectly well and costs less in storage, bandwidth and battery. If distance is the problem, optical zoom buys you more than resolution does — which is why the 4K RLC-811A is on this list for its 5x zoom rather than for its pixel count.
 Can someone steal a security camera and take the footage? + If the only copy is on a card inside the camera, yes. That is the honest cost of local storage and it is the one thing cloud recording genuinely does better. Three ways to manage it: mount the camera above easy reach, use a system where the camera streams to a recorder or base station kept indoors, or use a camera that records locally and optionally mirrors to cloud backup. A magnetically mounted camera at ground level is the worst case on this axis, which is exactly what the Tapo MagCam's skip line says.
 How many security cameras does a house need? + Count approaches, not rooms. A typical detached house has three or four ways to reach it: the front door, the back or patio door, the side passage and the driveway or garage. One camera per approach covers the property; one camera at the front covers the front. Adding contact sensors to the openings is far cheaper per covered point than adding cameras, and it answers a question cameras cannot — whether a door actually opened.
